title: Central management of connectors and MCP

opening.headline: Understand how to create a manageable connection structure by centrally managing department-specific connectors and MCP servers within an allowlist.
body: The sales team connected to the CRM, the development team to the issue tracker, and the HR team to the document repository. If the compliance team were to ask what external services are currently connected, it would be difficult to answer, as some products allow any user to connect to any desired MCP server by default.

In this lesson, we first confirm what an MCP is and how it connects to remote and private servers. Then we examine the MCP server access control patterns provided by Claude Code, including configurations that use allow and deny lists, and verification domain restrictions that prevent company data from being linked to personal accounts. Finally, we explain the procedure for approving custom connectors.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: We can describe the approach of managing connectors and MCP servers from a central location.
The allowlist and validation domain restriction each control different things.

screens.title: Each department made its own connector.
screens.lead: First, take a look at the structure of an organization where connections are dispersed across departments. It might help to consider whether the compliance team can answer the questions posed.

visual.alt: Three departments established connections to external services, and the overall list is missing.
labels: What external services are currently connected?

paragraphs: The sales team connected the CRM and AI tools to retrieve customer information. The development team built an MCP server to connect to the issue tracker, and the HR team separately established a document repository connection. These are reasonable choices based on each team's specific needs.

However, a problem emerges when the compliance team asks what external services are currently connected. There is no single document listing who created the MCP server and what permissions they hold. Moreover, Claude Code allows anyone to connect to any MCP server by default.

An important point is that simply being listed in the directory does not guarantee security. Anthropic reviews connectors against listing criteria before they are published in the directory, but does not perform security audits or provide oversight. Therefore, organizations must directly evaluate and determine which servers they allow.
The question to be answered in this class is this: What must be set where in order to control connections using a permit list?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: The goal is not to block connections. The goal is to know which connections exist and to allow only approved connections to be used. Without a list, neither option is possible.

screens.outro: Let's first consider whether our organization has an allowlist.

screens.title: Recall whether a list of allowed connectors exists
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Who is responsible for managing the list of approved connectors?
items.answer: Even if a list exists, it becomes misaligned with reality over time without designated owners. When a new server is needed, processes must be defined to determine who reviews the request and who adds it to the list. In this course explanation, we divide the responsibility into four stages: request, review, implementation, and verification.

items.prompt: What happens if you try to connect to a server outside the list?
items.answer: In environments where the allowed list is actually enforced, connection commands are rejected with a policy error. In environments where enforcement is not applied, the list is merely displayed as a guideline. Since list configuration and enforcement are separate concerns, both must be verified.

items.prompt: Is the path to connect company data to the connector using a personal account blocked?
items.answer: Personal accounts created with company email may allow company data to flow into external accounts such as Gmail or Drive. This pathway requires controls beyond the allowed list, and domain verification restrictions are the setting that specifically blocks this path.

screens.outro: First, I will clarify what MCP is and determine which connections should be treated as targets for control.

screens.title: MCP and Remote Server: What is Controlled?
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term in the description below to see a short description. Check the terms one by one.

visual.alt: The client inside the MCP host connects to the MCP server, and the private server communicates through a tunnel.

data.text: MCP is is an open protocol that enables AI apps to communicate with external services using standard methods. The program that exposes service functionality is MCP Server, and the AI app—specifically the client within host—connects to this server. Google Cloud provides Remote MCP server with governance, security, and access control, and can also publish its own MCP Server using Apigee or Cloud Run. OpenAI API allows developers to specify whether remote server tool calls are automatically enabled or whether they should be configured manually via Explicitly approved. If the server is located within an internal network, it connects without exposing it to the internet via Secure MCP Tunnel.

terms.tip: An open protocol abbreviated as Model Context Protocol, it is a standard method that enables AI applications to connect to external tools and data. Because the connection method is standardized, once a control framework is established, the same standards can be easily applied across multiple servers.

A program that exposes the functionalities of services such as APIs or databases as standard interfaces usable by AI applications. The capabilities of the server directly define the scope of risk associated with the connection.

This is the primary AI app that users create or use. Examples include tools such as Claude, VS Code, and Gemini CLI, where the client within the host is responsible for communication with the MCP server.

An MCP server accessible over a network. In some cases, it provides governance and access control similar to Google Cloud's remote server, while it can also be published to a self-hosted server on Apigee or Cloud Run.

This is a mechanism in the remote MCP tool of the OpenAI API that requires human or developer approval before executing tool calls. Conversely, automatic allowance proceeds with calls without approval and is only used with trusted servers.

This method connects servers located behind a firewall, private servers, or non-public servers without exposing them directly to the public internet. It is used when you want to connect AI products without exposing the servers.

screens.outro: Now let's compare the patterns for controlling MCP server access within Claude Code.

screens.title: MCP Server Access Control Pattern
screens.lead: The following table organizes the control patterns available in Claude Code in order of strength. Compare each pattern to see what it does and how it is implemented with specific settings.

data.caption: MCP Server Control Pattern and Configuration Methods
rows: MCP inactive
Does not retrieve any server other than the specified subset of servers
empty server map (mcpServers: {}) in managed-mcp.json
An organization that has decided not to allow MCP yet
fixed distribution
Provides only one server to all users and prevents adding additional servers.
The managed-mcp.json containing the desired server
An organization that must fully standardize its server configurations
Provided server
The remote server specified by the administrator is preferred, but the user's own server is also allowed.
Management settings' managedMcpServers
A standard server is a provider that allows autonomy within an organization.
Approval list
Only approved servers can be added; others are blocked.
allowedMcpServers and allowManagedMcpServersOnly: true
Organization focused on control based on an allowlist
Blocklist
Only block known risky servers and allow the rest.
deniedMcpServers
An organization that grants broad freedoms but blocks only risky servers
data.notes: managed-mcp.json is a separate file and cannot be deployed via server management settings; it must be deployed to the system path using device management tools such as MDM or group policy. Leaving allowedMcpServers empty is different from setting it to an empty array. If not specified, all servers are allowed; if set to an empty array, no servers are allowed.

screens.outro: Let's check the approval list method against the actual configuration file.

screens.title: Read approved list and denied list settings
screens.lead: The following are examples of approval and denial lists that can be included in management settings. Check the meaning by line number in the right-side description, and review the symptoms that appear when the settings are misconfigured.

notes.note: This is an allowed list. The remote server is specified as serverUrl, and a server that starts with standard input/output is specified as serverCommand. The serverCommand must exactly match both the command and its arguments in order. If only the remote server is specified using serverName, then the name serves only as a label assigned by the user and does not provide any control mechanism.

This is a blocklist. If the port portion is *, all ports are blocked; if no port is specified, only the default port 443 is blocked. If you attempted to block a server on a different port such as 8443 but did not specify the port in the pattern, the server will continue to connect. No configuration will allow access if it matches the blocklist.

If this value is true, the allowed list is only recognized from the management settings section. If this line is absent, the allowed list in the user's personal settings is merged, allowing the user to expand the scope. The list must be sourced from management settings to be enforced; attempting to add a server outside the list will display an error indicating that the server is not permitted by policy.

screens.outro: We will now proceed to examine validation domain restrictions, a control layer different from the allowed list.

screens.title: Verification domain restriction and product-specific connector control
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare the control locations when Claude Enterprise's validation domain restriction is enabled versus those of another product.

states.label: Claude Enterprise Domain Verification Limitation
states.body:
Enabling the restriction of verified-domain connectors to your enterprise means that Claude accounts outside of your enterprise organization will not be able to connect to supported connectors when using verified domain email from your company. The purpose is to prevent company data from being linked to personal Claude accounts.

Supported connectors include Gmail, Google Drive, Atlassian, Asana, Box, HubSpot, and others. This setting is managed at the parent organization level and applies to all child organizations, requiring at least one verified domain. There are limitations: since this check requires the connected service to share account identity, services that do not share identity will connect without undergoing this verification. Therefore, it is used in conjunction with other controls such as allowlists.

states.label: Control Location of ChatGPT·Gemini
states.body:
The location of connector controls varies by product. In ChatGPT Enterprise, administrators control app access and plugin installation separately through the Plugins section of the Admin Console. New plugins and apps are typically disabled by default, and access to plugins and included apps are governed by separate control mechanisms.

In Gemini in Workspace, Gemini features are enabled or disabled on a service-by-service basis in the Google Admin Console. Even if one app is disabled, access to its data may still be possible from another app, so simply turning off one app is not sufficient. Ultimately, control for any product never ends in a single location; organizing control locations by product is the first step toward centralized management.

screens.outro: Let's apply learned control to the custom connector approval procedure.

screens.title: Explanation: Custom connector approval process (1) Request and review
screens.lead: The instructor divides the process of handling a developer team's custom MCP server approval request into two parts. First, the request and review phase. Selecting the right arrow proceeds to the next step.

visual.alt: Approval process flow that undergoes review in the request, is reflected in the allowed list, and then proceeds to monitoring.

steps.title: Step 1: Request approval
steps.body: The development team has requested the use of a custom MCP server to connect with the internal issue management system. This request represents the first step toward requiring users to go through predefined channels rather than allowing them to add servers arbitrarily. With defined channels, records of which connections are requested can be maintained, enabling the audit team to respond when inquiries are made.

steps.title: Step 2: Fill in the request form with the operating entity, access scope, and data types.
steps.body: The request form specifies who operates the server, which systems are accessed and to what extent, and what types of data are handled. These three elements form the basis for review. Servers with unclear operators or broad access scopes are filtered out at this stage or require adjustments to narrow their scope.

steps.title: Step 3: Conduct security review
steps.body: Treat the server itself as a subject of audit. The fact that it is listed in the directory does not mean that a security audit has been completed; therefore, the organization directly evaluates it independently of its listing status. Verify whether the server exports data to external systems, how authentication is handled, and what tools are exposed.

steps.title: Step 4: Distinguish between read-only and write-permitted access.
steps.body: Based on the review results, we narrow the allowed scope. Servers that only query issues differ in risk from servers that create and modify issues. If read-only access is sufficient, exclude write tools and allow access accordingly; if write operations are required, add conditions requiring human approval. Safety is achieved by restricting permissions not at the server level, but by tool and scope level.

screens.outro: Let's move on to the second part, which involves actually reflecting and verifying the approved servers.

screens.title: Explanation: Implementation and verification of user-defined connector approval process (2)
screens.lead: The second part of the explanation. Follow the steps of listing approved servers, blocking those outside the list, notifying users, and checking the current status.

steps.title: Step 5: Add the approved server to the allowlist.
steps.body: Adds an approved server to the allowedMcpServers list. For remote servers, enter the exact address pattern in the serverUrl field. Using wide wildcards may inadvertently allow unauthorized servers, so it should be narrowed down as much as possible to specific paths and ports. Allowing access solely by name enables users to assign the same name to any server, resulting in lack of control.

steps.title: Step 6: Block servers outside the list
steps.body: By setting allowManagedMcpServersOnly to true, user-specific configurations are prevented from expanding the allowed list. If this setting is not present, the list follows the recommendations only. After this step, any attempt to add a server not on the list is rejected according to policy.

steps.title: Step 7: Inform the user about how the block will appear to them.
steps.body: When applying new restrictions, notify affected users in advance. When attempting to add a server, a message will appear stating that it is not permitted by policy, and existing servers may be removed from the list without any notice if they are blocked. By first informing users which server is being blocked, inquiries and confusion are significantly reduced.

steps.title: Step 8: Monitor the current connection status and compare it with the list.
steps.body: By configuring OpenTelemetry exporters, users can record which MCP server and tools are being invoked. The server and tool names are included in the records and aggregated by the collector, periodically compared against an allowed list to verify whether the actually used servers match the list. The list is not finalized after creation but is continuously compared against the current connection status and maintained accordingly.

screens.outro: We will consolidate and summarize the conclusion of the case on a single screen.

screens.title: Connectors are managed within an allowed list.
screens.lead: This summarizes the content reviewed so far as a benchmark for checking our organization's connectivity policy.

paragraphs: Managing connectors and MCP servers centrally means that an organization defines and enforces a list of connectable targets. The strength of control is divided into the following order: MCP deactivation, fixed deployment, provisioned servers, approval lists, and denial lists, and is adjusted according to the organization's autonomy and risk appetite. When using an allow list, the list must be locked in management settings with allowManagedMcpServersOnly to become enforceable.

Allow lists and validation domain restrictions serve different purposes. Allow lists control which servers can connect, while validation domain restrictions prevent company email account data from being connected to external account credentials. Since validation domain restrictions can only be enforced when the connecting service shares account identity, they are insufficient on their own.

Each product has different control locations. In Claude, it's management settings and organization settings; in ChatGPT, it's the Admin Console plugins; in Gemini in Workspace, it's service-specific settings. Blocking just one path may leave alternative routes available.

Finally, operations must be remembered. Custom connectors are processed in the order of request, review, implementation, and verification, and their connection status is periodically compared against the allowed list. Directory registration does not guarantee security, so the organization must evaluate it directly. With this procedure in place, the audit team can confidently respond to questions by stating that the currently connected external services match the allowed list.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Connectors are managed within an allowed list. A list must be created, enforced, and continuously compared against current status to maintain control.

glossary.def: A list that allows only approved connectors and MCP servers to connect.
This is a setting that prevents external accounts from connecting to a connector by using the company domain email.
It is the administrator's responsibility to define whether an MCP server is inactive, fixed, permitted, or denied.
This is an MCP server accessible via network. Private servers are connected without exposure to the internet, using a method similar to Secure MCP Tunnel.
A fixed MCP server configuration file deployed by the administrator via the device management tool, after deployment, users cannot add additional servers.

misconceptions.myth: The connectors listed in the directory are guaranteed to be safe.
misconceptions.fact: Registration review is different from a security audit or governance. Whether to allow a particular server must be directly evaluated and determined by the organization.

misconceptions.myth: Connector control ends at one point.
misconceptions.fact: Each product has a different control location. Claude covers management settings and organizational settings, ChatGPT covers plugins in the Admin Console, and Gemini covers product-specific settings.

misconceptions.myth: The allowlist is done once and done.
misconceptions.fact: Lists and actual connection statuses may become misaligned. Monitoring should be used periodically to compare the status against the list.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Connectors are managed within an allowlist.
Control strength is divided into inactive, fixed deployment, provided server, approval list, and denial list.
Verification domain restrictions prevent company data from being linked to personal accounts.
User-defined connectors are reviewed, listed, and verified through monitoring.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What control level does our organization's connectivity policy correspond to, and how are connections outside the list currently appearing?
